units.text: Parenthetical citations refer to the bibliography at the end. Philosophical texts are presented through interpretations and paraphrases, not translated quotations claiming a philological precision that is absent. Examples involving imaginary laboratories, communities, programs and observers are thought experiments constructed for this book. They do not represent empirical results.

Three levels will recur: what is well supported experimentally; what is a disputed philosophical interpretation; and what is a speculative hypothesis from which we can demand testable consequences. They are not three rungs of the same ladder. A mathematical proof is rigorous relative to its premises; an experiment connects a model to part of the world; a metaphysics asks what kind of world could make such connections possible.

‘Natural law’ can also designate a moral or legal doctrine. Here, ‘law of nature’ will primarily designate regularities and descriptive principles about the world. The transition from these to moral obligations will be discussed separately. That something happens is not, by itself, an argument that it ought to happen.
